newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mulls possible counter-claim against Iran.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mulls possible counter-claim against Iran.

text.p: The United States may sue Iran over damage to U.S. warships during the Iran-Iraq war if the International Court of Justice agrees this week to hear related Iranian claims against Washington, the U.S. State Department's top lawyer said on Monday.

Raising the prospect of a case with broad international implications, the department's acting legal adviser, Michael Matheson, said he would not be surprised if the court ruled it has jurisdiction over the pending Iranian claim. At issue is the destruction of three offshore Iranian oil platforms by U.S. warships almost 10 years ago.

"If that occurs ... we will have to consider whether ... we will bring a counterclaim against Iran for the damage done to American vessels during the course of that war. And that should be a very far-reaching case," he told an American Bar Association conference on national security law trends.

The court, an arm of the United Nations, was to rule on the jurisdiction issue on Thursday. Iran has charged that U.S. attacks on its oil platforms in October 1987 and April 1988 violated international law and the United States should pay damages.
Tehran took the case to the Hague-based court in 1992, arguing that a 1955 U.S.-Iranian Treaty of Amity and Commerce provided a legal basis for the court to settle the dispute.

Washington has urged the judges to throw the case out, calling its strikes a legitimate response to Iranian attacks on Kuwaiti-owned oil tankers sailing under the U.S. flag and a U.S. frigate damaged by a mine allegedly laid by Iran.

The dispute dates to the final stages of the 1980-88 war between Iran and Iraq when then President Ronald Reagan agreed to Kuwait's request to reregister 11 of its tankers under the American flag to benefit from U.S. Navy protection against Iranian attack. At the time, Iran viewed Kuwait as a belligerent because it aided Iraq financially and let arms bound for Iraq enter through Kuwaiti ports.

On Oct. 19, 1987, U.S. warships bombarded an offshore Iranian oil rig allegedly being used as a base for Iranian gunboats. It acted after an Iranian Silkworm missile hit a re-flagged oil tanker in Kuwaiti waters, injuring 18 crewmen.

U.S. Navy forces destroyed two more Iranian platforms after the U.S. frigate Samuel B. Roberts struck an underwater mine in international waters in the central gulf on April 14, 1988. The Roberts was returning from having escorted a U.S.-flagged Kuwaiti tanker as part of the convoy operation.
At hearings in September, the United States argued that its 1955 treaty with Iran governed commercial and consular affairs and that political and military matters fell outside its scope.

In an interview with Reuters after his remarks to the Bar Association forum, Matheson said the possible U.S. counterclaim against Iran probably would be filed "some time in mid-year" if the Iranian claim went to trial.
He said the pending Iranian case would involve the rules of naval warfare conduct and the rules of resort to use of force.
